backups.name: Spraying Mantis
hazards: Loose and sharp rock is a known issue at this recently-developed alpine sport crag.
The approach and crag sit in a remote basin with no cell coverage, so any injury means a long self-evacuation or SAR response.
backups.overview: Alpine sport climb at Sofa King Buttress in The Citidel area.
backups.beta: Fully bolted 100 ft (30 m) sport pitch rated 5.10b/c. The FA party (Wylie Moreshead) recommends starting left of the bolt line and straddling the low nose feature cheval-style rather than pulling straight onto it, keeping the rope managed on the inside leg to avoid an awkward twist. 12 bolts lead to chains at the top.
backups.turnaround: Not a big-mountain turnaround-time objective — the practical time constraint is the 20-30 minute approach through Silver Basin plus weather: the approach and base of the buttress are exposed, so turn back on the approach if lightning or fast-moving weather is closing in before you're committed to the rock.
backups.rappels: Single lower-off from chain anchors at the top; a 60 m rope is sufficient for this ~30 m route.
backups.comms: No documented cell coverage in this remote, forested Silver Basin approach off NF-9070; treat the area as a dead zone and carry a satellite messenger for emergencies.
backups.descent: Lower off the chain anchor at the top of the route.

backups.detailed_rack: Fully bolted: 12 bolts to a two-bolt chain anchor. No trad gear needed. A 60 m rope is enough to lower off the full ~30 m pitch.
what_to_bring: Helmet — rock at this new crag is still loose/sharp in places
Sturdy approach shoes for the talus/brush walk-in
Extra layer — Silver Basin can be cool and windy even in summer
pro_tips: Start left of the bolt line and straddle the low nose feature cheval-style rather than muscling straight over it, per the first-ascent party's own beta.
Keep the rope run on your inside leg through the straddle move to avoid getting twisted up.
watch_out: This is a newly-developed, "raw" crag — expect some loose or sharp holds and wear a helmet.
backups.pro_needs: Sport rack only — 12 quickdraws (plus 1-2 extra for the anchor). No natural/trad protection required or possible.
backups.best_season: June through October when FS Road 9070 is open and snow is minimal
backups.approach: From I-90 Exit 54 (Hyak), follow Hyak Drive onto Forest Service Road NF-9070, continuing past where the pavement ends to the junction at Ollallie Meadow where the Pacific Crest Trail crosses the road. Take the left fork of NF-9070 and follow it until the road terminates in a large turnaround just below Silver Basin. From that turnaround, it's roughly a 20-30 minute approach on foot up into Silver Basin to reach the base of The Citadel's walls, including Sofa King Buttress on the NW side of the basin's east wall. The road is not plowed and is generally only clear of snow from around July through November.
backups.descent_text: This is a single-pitch, fully bolted sport route with a chain lower-off anchor at its top; there is no walk-off. Thread/clip the chains and lower the full length of the route (a 60 m rope gives ample margin on this ~30 m line) back to the base.
backups.bail: The route is single-pitch and fully bolted, so retreat simply means lowering from the last bolt clipped (leaving a biner/draw if you don't have a way to clean while lowering) rather than a true multi-pitch bail.

pitch_detail.notes: 100 ft (30 m) bolted face pitch; starts with a cheval straddle over a small nose feature low down, 12 bolts to chain anchor.

backups.overview: Alta Mountain is a popular scramble on the long Rampart Ridge above Rachel Lake near Snoqualmie Pass. From the Rachel Lake trail and Rampart Lakes, an enjoyable Class 2 ridge walk and scramble leads along the crest to the summit with excellent views over the Alpine Lakes country.
backups.beta: From the Rachel Lake / Lila Lake trail junction, an unsigned 'climber's path' marked by a cairn leaves the maintained trail and climbs Alta Mountain's south ridge. The initial section is steep with loose rock and large steps and no shade; the grade then moderates onto a knife-edge ridge with sustained exposure. There are several class 2-3 moves, at least one 6-8 ft near-vertical step with good holds but serious exposure, a class 3 downclimb crux near the top, and multiple false summits before the true summit is reached. The route is non-technical (no rope typically used) but is exposed enough to be unsuitable for anyone uneasy with heights or for dogs.
backups.turnaround: Turn back if snow or ice is present on the ridge, if any party member is not comfortable with the class 3 downclimb crux or the sustained exposure, or if thunderstorms are building given the fully exposed ridge walk with no bail-out shelter.
backups.permit: Free self-issue Alpine Lakes Wilderness permit at the trailhead; no quota or fee. Northwest Forest Pass to park at most trailheads.
backups.descent: Reverse the ridge back toward Rachel Lake.
obj_haz: loose rock/scree on the climber's path
sustained fall exposure along the knife-edge ridge
a class 3 downclimb crux near the summit
no shade or water above Lila Lake

waypoints.directions: Trail #1313 runs beside Box Canyon Creek on gentle grade for roughly 2.75 miles, crossing several side streams and cascades — water is reliable the whole way, so there is no need to carry much from the car. Past the creek crossing the trail turns into the rooty, rocky boot-beaten climb locals call the 'mile from hell': about 1,300 ft of gain in a mile with large step-ups and no switchbacks. It is a fitness crux, not a technical one, but it is brutal under a full pack.

waypoints.name: Alta Mountain summit
waypoints.note: Reached past several false summits along the exposed ridge crest.
waypoints.directions: At the cairned fork on the Lila Lake trail an unmarked climbers' path leaves the maintained trail and follows the ridge crest toward the summit block. It starts steep, loose and shadeless with large steps, then eases onto a narrow crest with sustained exposure: expect several class 2-3 moves, at least one near-vertical step of six to eight feet with good holds, a short class 3 downclimb near the top, and three or more false summits before the real one. Do not attempt this stretch with snow on the crest or on wet rock — the path skirts a cliff edge and the fall consequences are serious. Helmets are worth wearing for the loose rock.

backups.detailed_rack: No rock rack is used or needed -- this is an unroped Class 2 hands-on-rock scramble, not a roped rock climb. Parties do not carry cams, nuts, hexes, or a rack of any kind on the standard South Ridge/Rampart Ridge route.

backups.pro_needs: None -- no technical protection is placed on this route. It is a Class 2 scramble: loose rock and large steps on the initial push, then a narrow, exposed but non-technical ridge crest with several false summits to the true summit. Rock quality on the ridge itself is solid enough for hands-and-feet scrambling; the main hazard is loose talus/scree on the lower approach slope rather than anything requiring gear placement.
backups.best_season: Mid-July through October (larch color in fall)
backups.approach: From the Rachel Lake Trailhead (2,800 ft, end of FS Rd 4930 off Kachess Lake Rd, Exit 62 from I-90), start on Rachel Lake Trail #1313. The first ~2.75 miles follow Box Canyon Creek on gentle grade, crossing several side streams and cascades (reliable water throughout — no need to carry much from the car). At about mile 2.75 the trail crosses Box/Canyon Creek and hits the notorious 'mile from hell': a heavily rooted, rocky boot-beaten climb that gains roughly 1,300 ft in about a mile, with large step-ups and no switchbacks — this is the crux of the approach fitness-wise, not technically hard but brutal with a full pack. The trail tops out at Rachel Lake (4,700 ft, ~3.5-4 mi from the TH); a use trail/climber's path branches right near the outhouse and skirts the north side of the lake, then switchbacks steeply up rocky tread for about half a mile to the Rampart Ridge crest (~5,100 ft). At the ridge junction, go left (south) for Rampart Lakes or right for Lila Lake/Alta Mountain — for this route, go right toward Lila Lake. The tread is brushy in places but easy to follow; after about 0.3 mile a cairn marks a fork where the Lila Lake trail continues straight and the unsigned climber's path to Alta branches left. Take the left fork, which starts steep and loose with big steps and no shade, and follow the increasingly exposed climber's path along the ridge crest toward Alta's summit block, negotiating three false summits, class 2-3 rock steps, and short sections of real exposure (in one section the path skirts a cliff edge — fall consequences are serious here, and the route should not be attempted with snow on the ridge). A helmet is commonly recommended for the final ridge scramble due to loose rock and exposure. Total one-way distance to the 6,274 ft summit is about 9.5-10 km (matches the 19.3 km round trip) with roughly 3,300 ft of total gain.
backups.descent_text: This is a scramble, not a technical climb — there is no rappelling on this route (rappels: 0). Descend by reversing the exact ascent line: retrace the ridge crest scramble back over the false summits and down the steep, loose lower ridge to the cairned fork, follow the Lila Lake trail back to the Rampart Ridge junction, drop via the steep half-mile rocky switchbacks to Rachel Lake, then retrace Trail #1313 down through the 'mile from hell' (this section is notably harder on tired knees going down — loose rocky step-downs and roots) and out along Box Canyon Creek to the trailhead. Key descent hazards mirror the approach: the exposed ridge-crest sections near the summit (do not descend this route if the ridge is snow-covered or wet — the exposed traverse becomes significantly more dangerous), loose rock on the steep lower ridge (rockfall risk onto anyone below — descend it one at a time), and the steep, rooted, ankle-turning tread on the 'mile from hell' switchbacks. No natural or fixed anchors are used anywhere on this route; parties should not carry a rope expecting to need it, though a short handline could be improvised on the steep lower ridge for less confident scramblers.
backups.bail: Descend off the ridge toward Rampart Lakes and the trail.

itinerary.cal: Snow can linger on the ridge traverses into July, and the route is not recommended in snow due to cliff-adjacent sections near the summit; best conditions are typically August-September.

days.note: Standard trip reports all treat this as a single long day hike/scramble, not a backpack. From the Rachel Lake TH (2,800 ft), hike Box Creek Canyon to Rachel Lake, climb to Rampart Ridge and turn right toward Lila Lake, then follow the unmarked climber's path up Alta's long south ridge past several false summits to the 6,274 ft summit. Reverse the same line to descend.

approach_variants.name: Rachel Lake, Rampart Ridge, and the cairned Alta turnoff on the Lila Lake trail
approach_variants.notes:
From the Rachel Lake trailhead at 2,800 ft, at the end of FS Rd 4930 off Kachess Lake Road from I-90 exit 62, take Rachel Lake Trail #1313. The first 2.75 miles follow Box Canyon Creek at a gentle grade with reliable water throughout.

At about mile 2.75 the trail crosses the creek and hits the section known locally as the mile from hell: a heavily rooted, rocky climb gaining roughly 1,300 ft in a mile with big step-ups and no switchbacks. It is the fitness crux of the day, not a technical one.

At Rachel Lake, 4,700 ft, a use trail branches right near the outhouse, skirts the lake's north side, and switchbacks steeply about half a mile to the Rampart Ridge crest at about 5,100 ft. At the ridge junction go right toward Lila Lake; the left branch leads to Rampart Lakes and is not this route. After about 0.3 mile a cairn marks a fork: Lila Lake is straight ahead, and the climbers' path up Alta's south ridge is the left branch.
approach_variants.season: July to October. The route should not be attempted with snow on the ridge
hazards: Sustained exposure along the ridge crest, including a section skirting a cliff edge
Three false summits and a class 3 downclimb crux near the top
Loose rock and large step-ups on the initial climbers' path
Afternoon thunderstorms on a long exposed crest
Lingering snow in the approach gully in early season
approach_variants.baseFinding:
The takeoff is a cairn on the Lila Lake Trail, not anything in the Rampart Lakes basin. At the ridge-top junction above Rachel Lake turn right (left goes to Rampart Lakes); about 0.3 mile along, a cairn marks a fork where Lila Lake is straight on and the unsigned climbers' path to Alta goes left. If you find yourself among the Rampart tarns, you took the wrong branch at the ridge.

Where it puts you: the climbers' path climbs Alta's south ridge, steep, loose and shadeless at first, before easing onto the narrow crest that leads to the summit block.

What the ridge then does, so you can count your way along it: three false summits, class 2-3 rock steps, at least one near-vertical step of 6 to 8 ft with good holds and serious exposure, and a class 3 downclimb crux near the top. A party that has crossed one bump and thinks it is at the summit is two bumps early.

And the one place where the finding is a warning rather than a direction: there is a section where the path skirts a cliff edge. Fall consequences there are serious. This route should not be attempted with snow on the ridge, and it is not a place for anyone uneasy with heights or for dogs.

A second, independent description of the same takeoff: an unsigned climbers' path marked by a cairn leaves the maintained trail near the Rachel Lake / Lila Lake junction and climbs the south ridge. Steep, loose, big steps and no shade at first, then it moderates onto the knife-edge crest.

bivy.name: Rachel Lake designated sites
bivy.notes: This is the base for Alta Mountain and for Hibox Mountain, and it belongs to a completely different approach than the Alpental peaks — I-90 exit 62 to Kachess Lake, then Box Canyon Road up to the trailhead at about 2,800 ft. The trail runs an easy few miles up Box Canyon Creek and then climbs hard and rootily to the lake at four and a bit miles. Alta is reached by continuing over the ridge crest above the lake; Hibox leaves the trail lower down, at around 3,300 ft, on a steep boot path onto Box Ridge. Both are day scrambles from the car for a fit party, so a night here is about a civilised start or a plan that ran long. The honest caveat is the state of the basin: it is one of the most hammered lake basins in the wilderness, the parking lot fills by mid-morning in summer, and the designated sites exist because dispersed camping wrecked the shoreline. Snow-free window is roughly July into October.
bivy.water: The lake and Box Canyon Creek are reliable all season. Treat it.
bivy.permit: Free self-issue Alpine Lakes Wilderness permit at the Rachel Lake trailhead, filled out at the box and carried for the trip. Camping is restricted to designated sites within half a mile of Rachel Lake and Rampart Lakes. Campfires are banned outright within half a mile of Rachel Lake and everywhere above 5,000 ft on this side of the crest, so plan on stoves regardless of where you end up. Party size capped at 12. Northwest Forest Pass or interagency pass for the trailhead, or a small daily fee. No drones. As of August 2026 the Box Canyon road and this trailhead were inside a wildfire closure order affecting a large part of the eastern Alpine Lakes; confirm the trailhead is actually open before driving to it.
bivy.capacity: Multiple established sites around the lake, but the basin is visibly damaged from decades of overuse and the hardened sites are what is left

bivy.name: Rampart Lakes basin
bivy.notes: A shelf of small lakes on the south side of Alta Mountain, reached by climbing north out of the Rachel Lake basin to the ridge crest at about 5,100 ft and then contouring west for most of a mile. Roughly six miles and 2,500 ft from the trailhead. For Alta Mountain's Rampart Ridge scramble this is better placed than Rachel Lake itself, since the ridge walk to the summit starts from the crest junction just above the basin rather than from the lake below it. Camping high also means camping exposed: the shelf is open, weather arrives with no warning, and there is nothing to shelter behind. Late July through September is the realistic season, and the basin is a well-known destination in its own right, so expect to share it.
bivy.water: The tarns hold water through the season. Treat it. They are shallow and warm late in summer, so draw from the inlets where you can.
bivy.permit: Same free self-issue Alpine Lakes Wilderness permit as Rachel Lake, from the Rachel Lake trailhead box. Designated sites only within half a mile of the lakes. No campfires anywhere above 5,000 ft on this side, and the whole basin sits above that line — stoves only, without exception. Party size capped at 12. Northwest Forest Pass or interagency pass to park. Subject to the same 2026 wildfire closure of the Box Canyon approach; check before committing.
bivy.capacity: Numerous established sites spread across the shelf between the tarns; more room than Rachel Lake but correspondingly busier on weekends

bivy.name: Kachess Campground, I-90 exit 62
bivy.notes: The drive-in answer for the eastern half of this zone, and the one you pass on the way to Box Canyon Road, so it is the sensible place to sleep the night before an Alta Mountain or Hibox Mountain day rather than driving over the pass at four in the morning. It is a lakeside family campground rather than anything resembling a climbers' camp, and it fills on summer weekends, so book rather than arrive hopeful. It sits low, on the shore of Kachess Lake, well below the trailhead. If it is full there is unreserved dispersed camping along the logging road toward the Rachel Lake trailhead, which is rough and unimproved but free and closer to the walk-in.
bivy.water: Drinking water is provided during the operating season.
bivy.permit: Standard campground fee, most sites reservable in advance and the remainder first-come. No wilderness permit required to sleep here and no trailhead pass needed for the campground itself. Seasonal operation only — it closes outside the summer months, so it is not a winter option. As of August 2026 this campground was among those closed by the wildfire order covering the north end of Kachess Lake; check it is open before relying on it.
bivy.capacity: Large developed Forest Service campground of roughly 150 tent and RV sites plus a group site; a mix of reservable and first-come, and very busy in summer

Unconsolidated snow over rock in the mid-route section.
Cold, committing winter conditions with limited daylight.
backups.overview: A mixed ice-and-rock winter line up Colchuck Peak's northeast face, right of the Northeast Couloir, combining two sustained AI3 ice pitches with technical M6 mixed climbing through a chimney system to the summit ridge.
backups.beta: The route starts with two 60m pitches of AI3 ice below a hidden couloir, then continues up and left on a few hundred feet of 50-60° snow. Two pitches of unconsolidated snow over moderate rock lead to a 30 ft leftward traverse into an M6 chimney (two pitches), followed by more steep snow and a final rock band to the summit area. A linkup variation ascends the Hidden Couloir and North Buttress to the northwest face.
backups.turnaround: As with any winter mixed route, turn around if ice quality is poor, avalanche danger is elevated, or the team can't reasonably top out with enough daylight/margin to descend the Colchuck Glacier.
backups.alpine_grade: Grade III (Alpine); FA account graded Grade IV
backups.rappels: No rappels specified — descend via the East Route down Colchuck Glacier
backups.face: Northeast Face, between the North Buttress Couloir and the Northeast Couloir
backups.permit: Enchantment permit area: overnight stays May 15-Oct 31 require a quota permit (Recreation.gov advance lottery); day trips need the free self-issued day-use permit at the trailhead.
backups.descent: Descend the East Route (standard route) down the Colchuck Glacier.
obj_haz: Technical M6 mixed climbing with sparse/thin protection
Unconsolidated snow over rock on the upper route
Winter climbing means very limited daylight
backups.detailed_rack: A light rack for M6 mixed climbing (small-to-mid cams and stoppers) plus 8 ice screws (2 stubbies, 6 x 10cm), 3 knifeblade pitons, and one picket for the upper snow.
what_to_bring: helmet
belay parka
approach skis or snowshoes (winter approach)
pro_tips: Best in condition in winter/early spring when the Hidden Couloir's ice pitches are fully formed.
watch_out: Mixed climbing crux — M6 chimney pitches with unconsolidated snow over moderate rock, plus a tricky M6 wide crack near the summit
Technical ice sections requiring solid mixed/ice climbing skills
backups.pro_needs: 2 stubby ice screws, 6x 10cm ice screws, 3 knifeblade pitons, 1 picket
backups.best_season: A winter/early-spring ice-and-mixed route, climbed roughly December through March when the Hidden Couloir's ice pitches are well formed; the first ascent was done in late January.
backups.approach: Hike the Stuart Lake Trail to Colchuck Lake, then continue to the base of the Colchuck Glacier/moraine below Colchuck's northeast face. The route starts right of the Northeast Couloir: two 60m pitches of AI3 ice gain the initial couloir, followed by several hundred feet of 50-60 degree snow trending up-left, then unconsolidated snow over rock, a short traverse left into an M6 chimney, and a final steep snow/rock band to the notch on the north ridge crest.
backups.descent_text: From the top of the route, join the standard East Route line and descend the Colchuck Glacier back toward Colchuck Col and Colchuck Lake, then follow the approach trail out.
backups.bail: Retreat by rappelling established ice/rock anchors back down the route, or downclimb easier snow via the adjacent Northeast Couloir if conditions allow.

pitch_detail.notes: Start right of the Northeast Couloir, at the foot of the Hidden Couloir. Two rope-stretching pitches of ice lead into the couloir. They take screws well when formed, and grades given range from AI3 to AI3+. This is the most reliable ice on the route; the ground above depends on winter snow conditions.
Leave the Hidden Couloir and climb a few hundred feet of 50–60° snow up and left toward a steep rock band. Protection is sparse, so carry a picket, and the slope loads with wind-drifted snow.

Two pitches of unconsolidated snow over moderate rock. Clear the snow to find placements for rock gear and pins, and move carefully: the snow gives little hold for tools, and a slip here runs down the slope below.
Traverse about 30 ft left into a chimney and climb two pitches of M6 mixed ground up it. Stubby screws, pitons and small cams protect it. This is the sustained technical heart of the route.
More steep snow leads to a final rock band. Climb through it to a notch on the north ridge crest.
Out of the north-ridge notch, a tricky wide crack at M6 is the last hard move. From its top, traverse around to the west into the final couloir of the North Buttress Couloir route.
Up the final couloir of the North Buttress Couloir line, one more short but steep mixed pitch reaches the summit, which is often rimed and windswept in winter. Descend by the Colchuck Glacier.

backups.itinerary: Typically climbed car-to-car in a single long winter day: approach via Colchuck Lake and the glacier basin (skis/snowshoes likely needed given the seasonal road closure), climb the AI3/M6 line to the summit ridge, then descend the standard East Route down the Colchuck Glacier.

access.fees: Day-use: free. Overnight lottery: $6 non-refundable application fee, then $5/person/night if selected. (Some approaches — e.g. Mount Stuart via Ingalls Creek/Longs Pass — fall entirely outside the Enchantment Permit Area and need only the free self-issue permit even overnight.)
access.notes: 2026 lottery application window Feb 15–Mar 1 (results after Mar 17, accept/pay by Mar 31). ~25% of overnight slots also released as a walk-up daily lottery the day before entry. Season requiring the overnight permit: May 15–Oct 31. A single-day ascent with no camp inside the boundary never needs the lottery.
access.rules: Overnight groups inside the permit boundary capped at 8 people, must camp together at one previously-impacted site, max 14 consecutive days, no re-entry same trip, permits non-transferable. Bear-resistant food storage mandatory forest-wide.
access.permit: Day climbs: free self-issue day-use permit at the trailhead — no lottery needed. Overnight camping inside the Enchantment Permit Area boundary: Enchantments overnight lottery permit (Recreation.gov).
access.closures: FR 7601 access road closed to vehicles all winter
access.landManager: Okanogan-Wenatchee National Forest, Wenatchee River Ranger District — Alpine Lakes Wilderness

access.parking_pass: Northwest Forest Pass required at Stuart Lake, Eightmile, and Snow Lakes trailheads — $5/day or $30/annual (overnight permit holders get a covering parking pass instead).
access.passRequired: Trailhead day-use fee/Interagency pass equivalent (when road is open)

overnight_permit.where: Apply in the February advance lottery or the daily lottery on Recreation.gov. The permit names one zone (Core, Colchuck, Snow Lakes, Stuart, Eightmile/Caroline) and you camp only there, except a Core permit, which covers every zone.

road.driveNote: Winter approach starts from the Icicle Road winter closure point near the Eightmile Road junction, well below the summer trailhead

climate.spring: Ice conditions can still be in shape into March; increasing avalanche hazard as freeze-thaw cycles begin.
climate.winter: Cold, short days, avalanche-prone approach; the route's defining ice typically forms this season.
climate.typical: Heavy Cascade winter snowfall; the northeast face holds ice/snow through winter and early spring.

emergency.notes: Winter rescues in this basin are especially slow given the gated access road and avalanche terrain; cell coverage in the basin is unreliable.
emergency.nearestHospital: Cascade Medical Center, Leavenworth (24/7 ED, ~20 mi from trailhead); Central Washington Hospital, Wenatchee, for higher-level trauma (~30 mi)
emergency.sheriffDispatch: 911 for emergencies (dispatched via RiverCom 911); Chelan County Sheriff non-emergency (509) 667-6851

seasonal_guidance.optimalWindow: January to February, during a stable high-pressure spell when the hidden couloir's ice is formed and the snow above has settled

May.reason: Spring melt strips the ice pitches and sheds rock down the face, and the overnight Enchantment permit season begins May 15.

April.reason: The ice start can still be climbable early in the month, but sun and warming rot the ice and raise avalanche and rockfall hazard.

March.reason: Longer days help, but warm spells start to soften the snow slopes and load the Colchuck Lake basin with wet slide hazard.

January.reason: The first ascent came in late January during a long high-pressure spell, which freezes the ice pitches and settles the snow above.

December.reason: Ice can form in the entry couloir, but short days and the unplowed road to the Stuart Lake trailhead make for a very long approach.

February.reason: Mid-winter cold keeps the AI3 and M6 chimney in shape; wait for a stable spell after storms to limit avalanche hazard in the basin.

November.reason: The AI3 start is usually not yet formed and early-season snow sits unconsolidated on the rock of the northeast face.

approach_logistics.trailheadDirection: From the Stuart Lake Trailhead (end of FR-7601 off Icicle Creek Road, ~3,400 ft), via the Colchuck Lake Trail

Kept Mountain Project's III/WI3 as the primary listed value since it reflects current guidebook consensus, with the AAC account's IV/AI3+ noted here as the FA party's own grading.

approach_variants.name: Colchuck Lake and the glacier to the ice below the Hidden Couloir
approach_variants.notes:
As for the other north-side lines: Stuart Lake trailhead, Stuart Lake Trail to the signed fork, right for Colchuck Lake and up the switchbacks to the lake at 5,570 ft, then the east-shore path to the inlet and up the basin to the Colchuck Glacier and moraine below the peak's northeast face.

In the season this route is in, expect the road to be gated well below the trailhead and the approach to be a longer day than the summer figures suggest. No trailhead-to-base time is given here because the known times are winter ones and vary too much to average.

Above the base the route runs two 60 m pitches of ice, several hundred feet of 50-60 degree snow trending up and left, then unconsolidated snow over rock, a short leftward traverse into a chimney at about M6, and a final steep band to a notch on the north ridge crest.

A variation climbs the ice start and then continues up the Hidden Couloir itself and across the North Buttress — a more sustained moderate line and a genuinely different day.
approach_variants.season: Winter and early spring, when the two ice pitches at the base are formed; the first ascent was in January
hazards: A winter approach with the road gated, in avalanche terrain above Colchuck Lake
Two rope-lengths of AI3 ice off the deck with committing ground above
Unconsolidated snow over rock above the ice — poor protection
An M6 chimney reached by a short traverse, with retreat from it difficult
Short winter daylight on a Grade IV route
Topping out on the north ridge crest, still a long way from the ordinary descent
approach_variants.baseFinding:
The Hidden Couloir is the marker and the route starts underneath it. This is the cleanest base identification on the whole face: find the Hidden Couloir, and the start is immediately below it — two 60 m pitches of good ice leading up to its base.

Position on the glacier, which is how you find the couloir in the first place: this line sits between the North Buttress Couloir and the Northeast Couloir. So walking up the glacier you pass the North Buttress Couloir first; the next thing is this. If you have already passed a second deep slot you have gone too high and are under the Northeast Couloir.

The positive test is the ice itself. This is the only line on the face that begins with two full rope-lengths of continuous ice off the deck. If the ground in front of you is snow, or mixed, or rock, it is not the start — whatever else it might be.

And the divergence above, because it is decided a couple of pitches up and not at the bottom: from the top of the ice this route goes up and left from the base of the Hidden Couloir onto difficult mixed ground. The variation instead climbs into the Hidden Couloir. Both start on the same ice. One is M6; the other is sustained moderate. Know which you have come for before you leave the second belay.

If you cannot find a couloir above your ice, you are not below the Hidden Couloir and should not assume the ice is the right ice.

bivy.name: Colchuck Lake designated campsites
bivy.notes: This is the working basecamp for Backbone Ridge, Serpentine Arete and Colchuck Balanced Rock, and it cuts an hour or more off the pre-dawn walk-in. Access is the Stuart Lake trailhead at the end of FR 7601, off Icicle Creek Road out of Leavenworth; the last few miles are rough dirt, washboarded by late summer, and the road is gated through winter and into spring. Parking is small for the demand, so a party arriving the night before should expect to be squeezed. Campfires are banned here, so plan on stoves only.
bivy.water: Reliable — the lake itself, plus inlet streams on the south shore through most of the season. Treat it; the shoreline is heavily used.
bivy.permit: Colchuck Lake zone of the Enchantment Permit Area. An overnight permit is required May 15–Oct 31 and comes either from the advance lottery on recreation.gov (applications open in February, success rates in the single digits) or the daily lottery run through the recreation.gov app inside a geofence around the Wenatchee River Ranger Station in Leavenworth. Day climbing needs no overnight permit, only the free self-issue Alpine Lakes Wilderness day slip at the trailhead and a parking pass.
bivy.capacity: Roughly a dozen scattered hardened sites around the east and north shores and up the west side; each permit covers one party, and group size in this zone is capped at 8

bivy.name: Bridge Creek and Eightmile campgrounds, Icicle Creek Road
bivy.notes: Given how unlikely a Colchuck or Core permit is on any given weekend, most parties on Backbone Ridge, Serpentine Arete or Colchuck Balanced Rock end up sleeping down on Icicle Creek Road and starting for the trailhead in the small hours. Both campgrounds sit on the drive in, before the FR 7601 turnoff, so the extra driving in the morning is only a few miles of dirt. Expect a very long day from here — car to base of route commonly runs three to four hours, and finishing after dark is normal.
bivy.water: Icicle Creek runs alongside both; check current potable-water status at the site, as it varies by year and season
bivy.permit: No wilderness permit at all — both are ordinary Forest Service campgrounds outside the Enchantment Permit Area, paid per night. This is what a party climbs from when it has no zone permit and is doing the route car-to-car, which is entirely legal: day use in the permit area needs only the free self-issue wilderness slip at the trailhead.
bivy.capacity: Bridge Creek is small and rustic; Eightmile is much larger with roughly forty family sites. Both take a mix of reservations and first-come nights depending on the season.

bivy.name: Talus and boulder bivies below Dragontail's north side
bivy.notes: Parties wanting to shorten the approach to Backbone Ridge or Serpentine Arete sometimes move above the lake into the boulders and moraine beneath the north face rather than staying at the shoreline camps. It buys perhaps half an hour and a clearer look at the route, at the cost of a colder, windier and rockier night. Whether that is worth it is genuinely contested: the time saved is small against a full day on either route, and the ground is poor. Because these are informal spots, camp on bare rock or gravel and leave no trace of a platform.
bivy.water: Snowmelt runnels and pools early in the season; unreliable by late summer once the snowfields shrink, so many parties carry water up from the lake
bivy.permit: Still inside the Colchuck Lake zone, so an overnight permit is required exactly as it is at the lake — sleeping on rock rather than in a designated site does not exempt a party. The zone boundary with the Core Enchantment zone lies up toward Aasgard Pass, and a Core permit is valid in every zone, so a party unsure which side of the line it will sleep on is safest holding Core.
bivy.capacity: Two to four people on flat granite blocks and sand patches; nothing established, and the good spots are scattered rather than clustered

backups.name: Southeast Ridge (from Lichtenwasser Lake)
gear: Trekking poles (summer)
Skis with skins or snowshoes (winter)
Avalanche transceiver, probe and shovel (winter)
Ice axe for firm spring snow
Map, compass and GPS with the bearings loaded — 177 degrees true to Lichtenwasser Lake, 248 degrees to the 5,640 ft saddle
Helmet (optional, for the loose ridge rock in summer)
hazards: Avalanche hazard on both the north and south flanks of the peak, with documented slide cycles on the north slopes below 5,000 ft and a history of large releases on the south side.
Cornice development along the summit ridge in winter and spring.
Steep timbered slopes and tree wells on the approach from the road to Lichtenwasser Lake.
Loose rock on the ridge crest above the saddle in summer conditions.
Whiteout navigation risk in the featureless forest between the road and the lake.
No cell coverage, no fixed anchors, and a 31-mile drive to the nearest 24-hour emergency department.
backups.overview: The short, direct line on Lichtenberg's northeast side and the peak's most-travelled route: a fishing trail to Lichtenwasser Lake at 4,708 ft, then open slopes southwest to a 5,640-foot saddle and an easy rocky ridge to the 5,844-foot summit. It is a rock scramble in summer and the classic Stevens Pass ski and snowshoe tour in winter.
backups.beta: This is the line described as a ridge that 'just screams skin me in winter'. In summer it is a 7-mile, 2,100-foot scramble starting from the first switchback on Smith Brook Road / FR 6700 and following the Lichtenwasser Lake fishing trail to a saddle on the southeast ridge. Jim Brisbine's party climbed it as a rock scramble over 20-21 September 1975, camping at Lichtenwasser Lake and continuing over the true summit to The Lichtenhorn before descending the west ridge. The winter version has you leave the road at the first major hairpin, head southwest up wooded and steep but always snowshoeable hillside, traverse toward Lichtenwasser Lake at about 4,600 ft (crossing the lake if it is frozen), then take easy slopes to the ridge crest and follow the summit ridge to the top. A winter north-side version is given with compass bearings: ski 2.6 miles up Smithbrook Road, leave it before the major switchback near 3,970 ft, follow a true bearing of 177 degrees to Lichtenwasser Lake, then 248 degrees from the lake's south end to a 5,640-foot saddle, and ascend the southeast ridge to the summit — about 5.2-plus miles, rated 2 to 2+ in skill and 2-minus in fitness, and included among the classic backcountry ski and snowboard routes in Washington. Avalanche hazard is the defining concern; both sides of the mountain present it.
backups.turnaround: Make the call on snow stability and visibility rather than the clock. Turn around if the slopes between Lichtenwasser Lake and the 5,640-foot saddle show any of the classic instability signs, if the NWAC Stevens Pass forecast is elevated and you would be travelling on or under steep open terrain, or if cloud drops low enough that you cannot hold your bearings between the lake and the saddle — this is compass-and-GPS country in a whiteout, with no landmarks in the trees. In summer, allow enough daylight to find the fishing trail again; missing it means a slow forested descent to the road.
backups.rock_grade: Class 2-3 rock scramble on the ridge above the 5,640 ft saddle; class 1-2 on the slopes below
backups.face: Southeast Ridge / northeast side above Lichtenwasser Lake
backups.comms: No cell service on Smith Brook Road above US 2, at Lichtenwasser Lake, or on the summit. Download offline maps and load your bearings or track before leaving the highway. Carry a satellite messenger; in winter this matters more than in summer, since a burial or injury here is time-critical and there is no way to call for help from the basin.
backups.descent: Reverse the southeast ridge to the 5,640 ft saddle and descend northeast to Lichtenwasser Lake and the road; skiers descend the same north-side slopes.

waypoints.name: Smith Brook Road (FR 6700) — first major switchback, start of the Lichtenwasser Lake approach
waypoints.directions: In summer, drive US 2 to the Smith Brook Road turnoff, Forest Road 6700, roughly 3.5 to 4 miles east of Stevens Pass around mileposts 68.7 to 68.9. Follow the unpaved road up toward the Smithbrook Trailhead and park at or near the first major switchback, where the Lichtenwasser Lake fishing trail leads off toward the lake. In winter FR 6700 is unplowed, so park on the shoulder of US 2 at or just before the Smith Brook Road turnoff and skin or snowshoe 2 to 2.6 miles up the snow-covered road, which is usually well packed by other parties. Start early on a winter trip so the road approach is behind you before the snow softens.

waypoints.name: Lichtenwasser Lake — camp and the launching point for the 248-degree bearing to the saddle

timing.recommendedStart: Summer: a mid-morning start is ample for this short day. Winter: start at first light — the 2 to 2.6 miles of road eat time on the way in, and an early start lets you be on and off the open slopes below the saddle before the day warms them.

backups.detailed_rack: No rock gear. Summer: trekking poles and boots with decent tread are the whole kit. Winter: skis with skins or snowshoes, plus the standard avalanche kit — transceiver, probe and shovel, worn and practised with, not carried as decoration. An ice axe is worth having in spring or after a freeze-thaw cycle for the firm slopes below the saddle; ski crampons help on the road and lower slopes when the track is icy in the morning.
what_to_bring: Offline topo maps and a downloaded GPX track
NWAC Stevens Pass avalanche forecast checked the morning of the trip
Satellite messenger
2 litres of water plus a filter (Lichtenwasser Lake in summer)
Insect repellent in July and August
Insulation and shell adequate for a windy summit ridge
Headlamp
Goggles and warm gloves in winter
Northwest Forest Pass for the dashboard
pro_tips: The road walk is the crux of the winter day, not the mountain. It is usually packed hard by other parties, so boots often work as well as snowshoes for the first 2 miles.

Load the compass bearings, not just a track: 177 degrees true from the road to Lichtenwasser Lake and 248 degrees from the lake's south end to the 5,640-foot saddle. The forested lower section is featureless in flat light.
Cross Lichtenwasser Lake directly if it is solidly frozen — it saves a slow traverse around the shore. Verify the ice first.
The north side generally holds better snow quality through the winter than the south, which is the main reason to prefer this line over the Yodelin approach.
In summer, camping at Lichtenwasser Lake makes this a relaxed overnight and lets you tag The Lichtenhorn as well as the main summit, which is what the 1975 party did.
If you want a circuit, climbing this side and descending south toward Yodelin works — but the south exit crosses private ground near the lodge, so ask permission before you leave a car there.
This route reaches the true 5,844-foot summit; the west peak (The Lichtenhorn, ~5,800 ft) is a separate top requiring a further scramble west along the ridge.
watch_out: Both flanks of the mountain present avalanche hazard, and the south side has been observed to release massive slides. Do not treat the moderate skill rating as a statement about stability.
The open bowl between Lichtenwasser Lake and the 5,640-foot saddle is the committing terrain — evaluate it before you enter it, not from partway up.
Cornices can form along the summit ridge; stay well back from the west and north edges in winter.
The lower forested slopes are steep enough in places to slide and hold tree wells; keep partners in sight.
Flat light in the trees makes the bearings essential; there are no reliable landmarks below the lake.
No cell service anywhere above US 2.
backups.pro_needs: None. There is no protectable rock climbing on this route and no fixed anchors anywhere on the mountain.
backups.best_season: This route has two seasons and both are good. Winter, roughly December through April, is the peak's main season and what this line is best known for — snow cover buries the brush and turns the whole thing into a straightforward skin and ski, and the north side holds the better snow quality through most of the winter. Summer and early autumn, July through October, give a short and pleasant rock and heather scramble; September is ideal, with the 1975 first documented ascent of the line falling on 20-21 September. Avoid late spring, when the snowpack is wet and heavy, avalanche hazard lingers on both flanks, and the ground below is still buried but no longer supportive.
backups.approach: Summer: drive US 2 to the Smith Brook Road / FR 6700 turnoff 3.5 miles east of Stevens Pass and follow the unpaved road up toward the Smithbrook Trailhead. Park at or near the first major switchback and find the Lichtenwasser Lake fishing trail, which leads roughly southeast then south through forest to the lake at 4,708 ft (47.7924, -121.0768). From the south end of the lake leave any semblance of path and climb southwest up open and lightly wooded slopes to the broad 5,640-foot saddle on the mountain's southeast ridge; turn right (northwest) and follow the ridge to the summit. Winter: FR 6700 is unplowed, so park on the shoulder of US 2 at or just before the Smith Brook Road turnoff, around mileposts 68.7-68.9 and 4 miles east of Stevens Pass, and skin or snowshoe 2 to 2.6 miles up the snow-covered road — it is usually well packed by other parties. Leave the road at the first major hairpin (near 3,970 ft), head southwest and then follow a bearing of 177 degrees true to Lichtenwasser Lake, crossing it when frozen, and continue on 248 degrees to the 5,640-foot saddle before finishing up the ridge.
backups.descent_text: The normal descent is a straight reversal: back down the summit ridge southeast to the 5,640-foot saddle, then northeast down the open slopes to Lichtenwasser Lake, and out on the fishing trail to Smith Brook Road. In winter this is the ski descent as well, and it is the reason the route is popular — the north side generally holds better snow through the season than the south. Two variants are known. Brisbine's 1975 party continued west over the true summit to The Lichtenhorn and descended the west ridge, which makes a traverse of the whole massif but commits you to trailless ground on the far side. There is also a circuit going up one side of the mountain and down the other, exiting south toward the Yodelin area near milepost 66.25, 1.3 miles east of Stevens Pass — that exit crosses private land near the lodge and homes, so ask permission before parking there. Whichever you choose, assess snow stability continuously before dropping into any steep slope: both flanks present avalanche hazard, and the south side in particular sheds massive slides from time to time.
backups.bail: Retreat is easy at every stage. From the summit ridge you can reverse to the 5,640-foot saddle in minutes, and from the saddle the fall line drops you back to Lichtenwasser Lake. The road approach means there is never more than a couple of miles of easy ground between you and the car. The real bail decision on this route is an avalanche decision rather than a terrain one: if stability is questionable on the slopes between the lake and the saddle, turn around at the lake — it is a fine destination in its own right — rather than committing to the open bowl above it. In winter, the packed road makes the return trivially fast even in bad weather.

pitch_detail.notes: From the lake's south end, climb southwest on a bearing of roughly 248 degrees true up open and lightly wooded slopes to the broad saddle on the southeast ridge. This is the avalanche terrain on the route and the section to assess carefully in winter; in summer it is easy walking on heather and scattered boulders.
pitch_detail.pitch: Section 1 - Lichtenwasser Lake (4,708 ft) to the 5,640 ft saddle

pitch_detail.grade: Class 2-3 rock scramble (easy snow ridge in winter)
pitch_detail.notes: Turn northwest at the saddle and follow the ridge crest to the 5,844-foot top. Short and easy, with a little hands-on scrambling on blocky rock when snow-free. Watch for cornices along the crest in winter.
pitch_detail.pitch: Section 2 - southeast ridge from the 5,640 ft saddle to the summit

backups.itinerary: Summer: a single easy day, roughly 4 to 7 miles round trip depending on where you leave the road, with about 2,100 to 2,600 ft of gain. Brisbine's party made an overnight of it in September, camping at Lichtenwasser Lake and taking in both the true summit and The Lichtenhorn the following day — a pleasant way to do it if you want an unhurried trip. Winter: a full but moderate day tour, about 5.2 to 8 miles and 2,100 to 2,700 ft of gain from US 2, with the road approach taking a good chunk of the time. Start early in winter to have the road walk behind you before the snow softens and to keep your options open on stability.

access.fees: The Forest Service lists no fee for the Smithbrook Trailhead site, and no permit is required for the north-side winter start on the US 2 shoulder. A Northwest Forest Pass is nonetheless reportedly expected at the trailhead — carry one if you park on the forest road.
access.permit: No permit or quota for day or overnight use in the Henry M. Jackson Wilderness here. Standard wilderness regulations apply; no mechanized travel.
access.closures: FR 6700 is unplowed and effectively closed in winter. The southern Yodelin start uses private parking and requires the owners' permission. Campfires are prohibited at Lake Valhalla and discouraged throughout the wilderness.
access.landManager: Okanogan-Wenatchee National Forest, Wenatchee River Ranger District, Leavenworth — (509) 548-2550. Lichtenwasser Lake and the summit lie within the Henry M. Jackson Wilderness.
access.passRequired: Northwest Forest Pass or America the Beautiful recommended for the FR 6700 trailhead; no pass needed for the winter US 2 shoulder parking.

road.name: Smith Brook Road / Forest Road 6700
road.status: Unpaved and passable to passenger cars in summer, roughly 2.5-3 miles from US 2 to the Smithbrook Trailhead at about 4,000 ft; this route leaves it earlier, at the first major switchback near 3,970 ft. Not recommended for stock trucks or trailers.
road.driveNote: From Stevens Pass drive 3.5 miles east on US 2 and turn left (north) at the FR 6700 sign; from Leavenworth drive 31 miles west and turn right. In winter, watch for the large pullout on the highway shoulder about a quarter mile before the Smithbrook sign. The alternative south-side start near Yodelin (milepost 66.25, 1.3 miles east of Stevens Pass) uses private parking and requires permission from the lodge or homeowners.
road.seasonalGate: Unplowed and impassable to vehicles once snow arrives. Winter parties park on the US 2 shoulder at the Smith Brook Road turnoff, roughly milepost 68.7-68.9 and 4.2 miles east of Stevens Pass, and travel 2 to 2.6 miles of snow-covered road on foot, snowshoes or skis; it is usually packed by prior traffic.

climate.fall: Excellent. Cool, dry, bug-free and with firm footing; the 1975 documented ascent was on 20-21 September. The window closes with the first substantial snowfall, usually late October or November.
climate.spring: Wet, heavy maritime snowpack and continuing avalanche hazard on both flanks. The road melts out ahead of the mountain, giving a long dry approach to a still-snowbound peak — an awkward combination and the least attractive season on this route.
climate.summer: Snow-free from about early July. The fishing trail to Lichtenwasser Lake is straightforward, the upper slopes are heather and boulder walking, and the ridge is a short easy scramble. Bugs are heavy at the lake in July and August.
climate.winter: The route's headline season and a listed classic backcountry ski tour. Snowfall makes the ridge easy to skin, and the north-facing approach generally holds the better snow. Avalanche hazard is present on both sides of the mountain throughout; consult the NWAC Stevens Pass forecast and reassess continuously in the field.
climate.typical: Marine west-coast climate with heavy Pacific precipitation, predominantly winter snowfall. Just east of the crest, so snow here is typically a little drier and colder than on the west-side slopes, and the north-side approach used by this route holds better quality snow than the sun-exposed south flank.
climate.forecastZone: NWAC Stevens Pass avalanche and mountain-weather zone; Okanogan-Wenatchee National Forest, Chelan County

emergency.notes: No cell coverage above US 2, so an avalanche or injury response depends on a satellite messenger or on someone travelling back to the highway. Stevens Pass, 4 road miles west, is the nearest developed point. In winter the route is popular enough that other parties are often on the road, but the slopes above Lichtenwasser Lake can be empty — never rely on being found.

May.reason: Late spring brings rotten, unsupportive snow over buried ground and lingering wet-avalanche hazard on both flanks.

April.reason: The snowpack turns wet and heavy, the lake ice becomes unsafe, and brush starts to reappear low on the approach.

March.reason: Longer days and still-deep snow, but warming raises wet-slide and cornice hazard, especially on the south side.

January.reason: Deep cover buries brush and talus, the lake is usually frozen to cross, and the north slopes hold good snow; watch for cornices on the ridge.

December.reason: The unplowed Smith Brook Road is usually packed for skinning and snow is filling in the forest, but early-winter slide cycles are common.

February.reason: Deepest snowpack and good north-side snow make the classic skin to the 5,640 ft saddle; check avalanche danger on both flanks.

November.reason: Early snow may not yet cover the brush and timber between FR 6700 and Lichtenwasser Lake, and the lake is not reliably frozen.

September.reason: A pleasant snow-free rock and heather scramble via the fishing trail, but a different outing from the ski line this route is known for.

gear: Rack to 5 inches (single set)
BD #4 cam (optional, for upper slab)
hazards: Loose or friable ('choss') rock typical of the broader Monte Cristo climbing area.

backups.overview: A one-pitch 5.7 trad line up Mossy Loaf's lower tier, climbing an open-book past a distinctive 'monkey face' rock feature to a roof, then a steep lieback flake crux before easing off on slab.
backups.beta: Follows an open book formation through moss and ferns. Climbers pull a feature nicknamed 'Harambe's nose' to reach a block above and right of a monkey-face visible in the rock, then proceed under a roof overhang (placing gear), traverse left into an 'awesome lieback flake' — the 5.7 crux — and finish up easier slab. The route is named for the monkey-face feature in the wall.
backups.turnaround: Not an alpine turnaround-time situation given the roadside single-pitch length, but the wall is shaded and moss/fern-covered — if holds are wet or slick after rain, back off before committing to the lieback crux rather than pushing through greasy rock.
backups.permit: Free self-issue Henry M. Jackson Wilderness permit or trailhead registration; no quota or fee. Northwest Forest Pass at developed trailheads.
backups.descent: Walk off along the base of the tiers back to the roadside; no fixed rappel anchor is documented for this single-pitch line.

backups.detailed_rack: Standard trad rack to 5 inches; a single Black Diamond #4 cam is useful near the top and could allow running out the final easier ground.
what_to_bring: A stiff brush for lingering moss on holds
Helmet — Monte Cristo-area rock is generally chossy
pro_tips: The route's name comes from a monkey-face feature in the rock passed partway up, near the 'Harambe's nose' hold.
Route developers cleaned the line but note it remains naturally mossy — expect some residual moss/lichen off the main hold line.
watch_out: Holds can be damp or moss-covered after rain given the shaded, fern-covered character of the wall.
General Monte Cristo-area rock is described as chossy/friable — test holds before committing.
backups.pro_needs: Gear to 5 inches; solid finger-to-hand-size placements protect the lieback-flake crux and the roof traverse best.
backups.best_season: Developers describe the wall as naturally mossy even after cleaning; drier summer-into-early-fall conditions (once accumulated winter/spring moisture has had time to dry out) will generally offer the cleanest holds, though no specific climbing-season window is published for this crag.
backups.approach: From the Barlow Pass gate, walk the closed road (old railroad grade) approximately 4 miles to the Monte Cristo townsite; a backcountry campground sits at that mark. Mossy Loaf's coordinates place it essentially at/immediately adjacent to the townsite itself, so once at the flat of Monte Cristo the formation is only a short distance further off the main townsite path. The exact final spur to the specific wall is not well established, so on-site scouting is recommended for the last stretch.
backups.descent_text: From the top of the route, downclimb the easy slab above the crux or scramble off along the wall's edge back to road level. The standard walk-off between tiers involves some bushwhacking, which is one reason the neighboring route You Moss Be Joking exists as a lower-impact link.
backups.bail: Single pitch, only 45 ft: retreat by downclimbing the easier slab above the lieback crux, or build a gear anchor and lower/rappel on trad protection — no fixed hardware is documented on this route.

pitch_detail.notes: Open book past the 'monkey face' feature to a block, then left onto the lieback flake (crux), finishing on mossy slab.

backups.fa: Everett and Ida Darr, 1940 (first ascent of the peak)
gear: Helmet (loose rock/rockfall is a real hazard on the summit pyramid)
30 m rope for rappelling the crux and upper pyramid
Light rack (a few small cams/nuts) for optional protection on the crux

backups.overview: Tupshin Peak (8,347 ft) is one of the 'Stehekin Seven,' a knot of rarely visited summits above the Stehekin valley in the Glacier Peak Wilderness. The mountain is built of several rock turrets running south, east, and northwest from a central high point roughly 200 ft above its neighbors. First climbed in 1940 by Everett and Ida Darr, it's approached entirely by boat and trail (no road reaches the peak). The standard line climbs the broad south ridge/upper east face to a short, exposed, and notably loose class 4-to-low-5th crux through old gneiss just below the summit.
backups.beta: From Bird Creek Camp, climb NNE up open sub-alpine slope to a broad shoulder (~7,000 ft) on Tupshin's lower South Ridge, then traverse/descend slightly around cliff bands into the upper east basin (~7,500 ft) below the face — about one mile from Bird Creek to the base of the climbing. The basin is a talus fan, often snow-covered early season. From there, rambly Class 2-4 terrain and a short crux (5.2-5.4, on a flake/crack) lead through the face to Class 3-4 summit-pyramid scrambling and the top. Multiple parties describe this same basic line with minor route-finding variations near the crux.
backups.turnaround: Given the long, remote approach and a descent that is itself technical and routefinding-heavy, set a firm turnaround time from camp that leaves ample daylight to complete both the summit climb and the rappel/downclimb descent — at least one recorded ascent summited in the evening and did not finish descending until after midnight by headlamp.
backups.rock_grade: Class 4-5 (low 5th class scrambling; no specific YDS number grade attested)
backups.rappels: One short rappel reported near the summit (~30 m rope sufficient) off an old webbing anchor; back it up before weighting
backups.permit: Free self-issue Glacier Peak Wilderness permit at the trailhead; no quota. Northwest Forest Pass at many trailheads.
backups.comms: No reliable cell coverage in the Devore Creek/Bird Creek drainage or on Tupshin's upper mountain. A satellite messenger (e.g., Garmin inReach) is strongly recommended — regional Chelan County SAR operations in this area have relied on inReach activations to trigger helicopter response.
backups.descent: Reverse the route: downclimb and rappel the loose summit pyramid and crux back to the south-ridge shoulder and Bird Creek basin.

backups.detailed_rack: A light rock rack is sufficient for the crux and any protected pitches: a set of small-to-mid cams, a few nuts, and several slings/draws, plus a 60m rope for the crux pitch and descent rappels. Some parties have soloed sections in rock shoes; others have pitched out the crux and upper face with a full rack.

pro_tips: Bring a rope even if confident — the crux exposure justifies it
Budget extra time for the remote Stehekin approach and brush
watch_out: Ropes snag easily in the loose rock on rappel — a single-strand rappel is usually preferable to a doubled rope
Devore Creek Trail blowdown can turn the approach into a multi-hour bushwhack in bad years; check current trail conditions with the Chelan Ranger District first
backups.pro_needs: A short rope and a light rack are advisable for the exposed class 4 / low-5th crux; many parties belay the steepest step.
backups.best_season: Snow typically lingers in the Bird Creek basin and on the upper route into July, so mid-July through September is the reliable window; early-season parties should carry an ice axe for lingering snowfields, while late-season parties get drier but no less loose rock. Check regional Cascades snowpack/NWAC data before an early trip.
backups.approach: No road reaches the mountain. Take the Lady of the Lake or Lady Express passenger ferry from Fields Point Landing up Lake Chelan to Stehekin Landing, then ride the Stehekin shuttle bus (or walk) roughly 4.4 miles up-valley to Harlequin Bridge, cross it, and continue about 3 more miles on the Stehekin River Trail toward Weaver Point to the signed Devore Creek Trail junction (about a half mile before Weaver Point). Follow the Devore Creek Trail as it switchbacks up into the Glacier Peak Wilderness (Okanogan-Wenatchee National Forest); it is brushy but generally passable toward Tenmile Pass, though blowdown has been significant in some years — check current trail conditions with the Chelan Ranger District before you go. Leave the maintained trail and work up the ridge north of Bird Creek through steep brush, slide alder, and blowdown (about 1,000 ft of gain with little real open forest) to a good camp with running water in the lower Bird Creek basin, roughly 5,400-5,800 ft. The boat-landing-to-camp day is reportedly around 10 miles and 5,000 ft of elevation gain.
backups.descent_text: Reverse the climb: rappel (single-strand preferred over doubled rope to avoid snagging in the loose rock) and downclimb the crux and upper pyramid back to the 7,000-ft shoulder, then descend through the talus and brush back to the Bird Creek basin camp. From camp, reverse the bushwhack to the Devore Creek Trail, then the Stehekin River Trail to Harlequin Bridge and Stehekin Landing for the return ferry — plan the trip around the ferry schedule, since missing the last boat means an extra night in Stehekin.
backups.bail: Retreat down the ascent route; rappel the crux.

pitch_detail.notes: Bird Creek Camp NNE up open sub-alpine slope to the broad shoulder (~7,000 ft) on the lower South Ridge, then a slightly descending traverse around cliff bands into the upper east basin (~7,500 ft).
~1 mile across a talus fan, often snow-covered in early season, to the base of the technical climbing.
Rambly, somewhat loose rock; a short (~20 ft) Class 4 step is a common first obstacle en route to the upper face.
Short crux section on a flake/crack system gaining the upper face; protection is sparse and 'dubious.'
Class 3-4 gully/scrambling for the final distance to the true summit.

access.fees: Round-trip Lady of the Lake/Lady Express passenger ferry fare from Fields Point Landing to Stehekin (check current rates at ladyofthelake.com); the in-valley Stehekin shuttle bus runs about $10/adult one-way (2026 rate, Stehekin Valley Adventures) if you don't walk from the Landing to Harlequin Bridge. The wilderness permit itself is free.
access.permit: Once past the NPS boundary, a free, self-issued Glacier Peak Wilderness permit (available at the trailhead, no reservation or fee) covers the climb and Bird Creek camp. If you camp overnight anywhere within the Lake Chelan NRA/Stehekin corridor before reaching the wilderness boundary, an NPS backcountry permit is required (reservable via recreation.gov or in person at the Golden West Visitor Center in Stehekin).
access.closures: Stehekin suffered major flooding and landslides in December 2025 — a levee failure sent the Stehekin River into Company Creek Road near Harlequin Bridge — with a further damaging flood event in March 2026; recovery work was still ongoing into summer 2026. As of June 2026 the Stehekin Valley Road was reported open from the Landing to Stehekin Valley Ranch, but check the NPS 'Stehekin Flood Response Update' page and the Chelan Ranger District before a trip, since the Harlequin Bridge/Devore Creek approach corridor was directly affected by the flood. Sisi Fire: Okanogan-Wenatchee National Forest closure order 06-17-02-2026-35 (Sisi Fire), in effect August 22 through December 31, 2026 unless lifted sooner, closes Devore Creek Trail 1244 from where it enters the national forest to Hilgard Pass, the 4th of July Basin Trail 1244.1 and Company Creek Trail 1243. This approach cannot be used while the order stands. Chelan Ranger District: (509) 682-4900.
access.landManager: The lower approach (Stehekin River Trail near Harlequin Bridge and the Devore Creek trailhead) lies within the North Cascades National Park Service Complex — Lake Chelan National Recreation Area (NPS). The Devore Creek Trail then crosses into the Glacier Peak Wilderness on the Okanogan-Wenatchee National Forest (Chelan Ranger District) for the climb itself.
access.passRequired: No Northwest Forest Pass needed at this boat-in trailhead; wilderness permits (above) are the operative requirement.

approach_variants.name: Stehekin, Devore Creek and the Bird Creek basin
approach_variants.notes: No road reaches this mountain. A passenger ferry up Lake Chelan to the landing, then a shuttle or a walk up-valley to the bridge, then the river trail to the signed Devore Creek junction about half a mile short of the campground. The Devore Creek trail switchbacks up into the wilderness and is brushy but passable, though blowdown has made it a multi-hour fight in bad years, so check the current state before committing. Leave the maintained trail and work up the ridge north of Bird Creek through steep brush, slide alder and downed timber — roughly a thousand feet of gain with very little open forest — to a camp with running water in the lower basin somewhere between about 5,400 and 5,800 ft. Plan the whole trip around the boat schedule; missing the last one costs a night.
hazards: Loose, rockfall-prone gneiss on the summit pyramid, which releases spontaneously as well as under a boot
A brutal, largely trailless bushwhack between the maintained trail and the basin camp
A snow finger at the foot of the cliff that lingers unexpectedly late — carry an axe and consider crampons
Exposed class 4 and low-fifth climbing that most parties do with minimal protection
Ropes snag badly in the loose rock on rappel, so a single-strand rappel is usually preferable
Remote and multi-day with no cell service in the valley
approach_variants.baseFinding: From the basin camp climb north-northeast up open subalpine slope to the skyline shoulder at roughly 7,000 to 7,200 ft, where the summit pyramid comes fully into view for the first time — that view is the checkpoint, and if you cannot see a distinct pyramid you are not yet on the shoulder. From there traverse and drop slightly around the cliff bands into the upper basin on the east side, at about 7,500 to 7,600 ft. The base is the talus fan at the foot of a continuous cliff band that runs unbroken to the top, and it is marked by a snow finger that sits at the very bottom of the wall and survives most summers. Start the climbing from that fan. The common error here is drifting too far east across the basin and starting up loose ground well right of the line; if the rock is uniformly rotten and you are hugging the skyline on your right, work back left toward the east ridge to regain the route.

bivy.name: Bird Creek Camp, Devore Creek trail
bivy.notes: This is the camp for Devore Peak and Tupshin Peak, and it is worth being clear that these two are not a Sawtooth trip. They stand west of Lake Chelan on the long ridge dividing Company Creek and Hilgard Creek from Devore Creek, and everything about them - the wilderness, the permit system, the transport - is different from the Twisp River peaks. The usual way in is a ferry to the Stehekin landing, then the Company Creek road, with the Devore Creek trail reached from Weaver Point on the far side of the head of the lake; Bird Creek Camp sits about four miles up that trail at around 4,200 ft. From here Tupshin's South Ridge and Devore's Southeast Ridge are both reachable, and parties commonly climb both from the same base, either from this camp or from a higher bivouac around 5,800 ft in the Bird Creek basin. Both are steep, brushy and loose by reputation and neither is a walk-up. The season is roughly late July into early October; the approach is low, hot and overgrown early, and the upper slopes hold snow. This is the least forgiving logistics in the zone - a party that misses a boat or a bus loses a day at each end - so build slack into the itinerary and carry more food than the schedule strictly needs.
bivy.water: Bird Creek is immediately past the camp; the site sits about a hundred feet short of the crossing. Below here, Devore Creek is the last dependable water on the climb, so fill there if you are unsure. Parties going higher can camp near 5,800 ft in the Bird Creek drainage, where there is water in early and mid-season but which can dry out late.
bivy.permit: This is inside the Lake Chelan National Recreation Area, so a North Cascades backcountry permit is required year-round for the overnight, tied to a specific camp and itinerary. Peak-season demand is high enough that an early-access lottery governs the best dates and the odds are poor; plan around it rather than hoping. Open fires are banned at several camps in this unit and restricted to established pits elsewhere, and a total ban is normal by late summer. The ferry and the Stehekin shuttle are the other half of the planning: the boat must be booked, the shuttle up the valley runs a limited seasonal schedule, and the Company Creek road trailhead is several miles from the landing, so missing a bus costs you a half day on foot.
bivy.capacity: Three small tent openings and a fire ring - room for perhaps four small tents. Very small, and there is no overflow.

backups.overview: Mount Seattle (6,246 ft) rises deep in the Olympic interior, about 7.5 miles southeast of Mount Olympus, within the Daniel J. Evans Wilderness of Olympic National Park. Its northeast aspect drops over 3,800 ft to the Elwha valley in only about 1.5 miles, but the standard scramble routes stay on the gentler south/west scree and talus slopes. The peak was named April 29, 1890 by James Halbold Christie and topographer Charles Adams Barnes of the Seattle Press Expedition, in honor of the city that sponsored their winter crossing of the range; it was first climbed in 1907 by Asahel Curtis, Grant Humes, and Lorenz Nelson while reconnoitering for a climbing club's first attempt on Mount Olympus. Reaching the base of the peak requires a long, committing wilderness approach from either the Elwha or North Fork Quinault drainages — there is no easy day-trip line to this summit.
backups.beta: Most parties base-camp at Seattle Meadows (~4,550 ft), reached via a multi-day approach up the North Fork Quinault River to Low Divide and then west into Seattle Creek Basin. From camp, climb scree slopes on the mountain's western side, cross over a ridge, and continue up scree and talus on the eastern side, finishing with a class 2-3 scramble on the east ridge/side to the craggy summit. Two other approach variants exist (via Noyes Basin, and a more direct line up Seattle Creek Basin itself), converging on the same upper-mountain scramble.
backups.turnaround: Because the upper mountain is loose scree/talus with real rockfall and slip potential, and the approach is long and entirely off-trail through remote wilderness, set a firm turnaround time before starting the summit push and commit to it — visibility loss (fog/cloud) on the unmarked upper slopes is the biggest threat to a safe descent, and there is no faster way down than the way up.

backups.pro_needs: No technical protection is documented for this route — it is an unroped Class 3 scramble with no glacier travel per the published route description.
backups.approach: Two realistic approach corridors exist, both multi-day: (1) North Fork Quinault side — from the North Fork Quinault Trailhead at the end of the North Shore Road (not the South Shore Road, which leads to Graves Creek and the East Fork instead), follow the North Fork Quinault River Trail or the higher, rougher Skyline Ridge Primitive Trail (via Three Lakes and Kimta Peak) to Low Divide, 16 miles one-way by the river trail and much farther by the ridge, then cross-country/climbers'-path to Seattle Meadows below the peak's south side. (2) Elwha side — from the Whiskey Bend trailhead (the road to it has been closed to vehicles at Madison Falls since November 2017 flood damage, adding about seven miles each way on foot or bike), follow the Elwha River Trail up the Elwha valley toward Elwha Basin/Low Divide (on the order of 20+ miles one-way), then leave trail to climb into Seattle Creek Basin or Noyes Basin on the peak's northeast side. Either way, plan on a multi-day backpack just to reach a base camp, with several thousand feet of trail gain before any scrambling begins. The Seattle Creek Basin approach (Elwha side) follows the creek's waterfalls until the drainage steepens, forcing a steep, brushy bushwhack up onto the Mt. Noyes-Mt. Seattle ridge — expect slow going in heavy brush low down.
backups.descent_text: Descend the ascent line in reverse: downclimb the east ridge scramble back to the scree/talus on the east side, cross back over the connecting ridge, and descend the west-side scree to Seattle Meadows camp. The scree and talus are loose and unconsolidated in places, so downclimb carefully rather than trying to glissade or boot-ski except where lingering early-season snow makes it safe; rockfall onto parties below is a real concern on the looser sections.
backups.bail: Reverse the scramble; no fixed anchors required.

access.fees: Olympic NP wilderness permit reservation: $6 reservation fee plus $8 per person per night for climbers/backpackers age 16+ (15 and under free), as of 2026.
access.notes: No separate climbing cost-recovery fee like Mount Rainier’s $82 — only the standard entrance fee and wilderness camping permit apply.
access.rules: Hard-sided, approved bear-resistant food canisters are required for all overnight stays throughout most of Olympic Wilderness, including the Elwha and Quinault interior zones; bear wires/hangs are not accepted. There is no separate climbing registration — rangers do not certify competency or refuse a permit for lack of gear/experience, so self-sufficiency and route knowledge are entirely on the party.
access.permit: A backcountry wilderness camping permit is required for any overnight stay and must be reserved through recreation.gov before your trip.
access.closures: Olympic Hot Springs Road beyond Madison Falls has been closed to vehicles since November 2017 flood damage, with no reopening date on Olympic National Park's alerts page updated August 27, 2026, adding roughly 7 miles each way of walking or biking to reach the Whiskey Bend trailhead on the Elwha approach. On the Quinault side, South Shore Road has a separate washout closure near milepost 8 (use North Shore Road as the detour); North Shore Road itself also had a seasonal construction closure near milepost 10.2 (culvert replacement, closed July 9–Sept 22, 2025). Call the park's Road and Weather Hotline (360-565-3131) or check nps.gov/olym for current status before committing to either approach.

approach_variants.baseFinding: The staging point is Seattle Meadows, the high camp in upper Seattle Basin about a thousand feet above Seattle Creek. There is no gully mouth to find here: from camp the climb starts on scree on the mountain's western side, and the base is simply where meadow gives way to loose scree and the slope steepens. What identifies the route is the sequence, so hold it in mind — climb the west-side scree, cross over a connecting ridge, then continue up scree and talus on the eastern side, and finish with Class 2 to 3 scrambling on the east ridge to a craggy top. If you are still high on the west side and the ground is cliffing out above you, you have failed to make the crossing and need to traverse. The summit is confirmed by an unusually large plastic tube jammed into a crack holding the register. Coming instead up Seattle Creek Basin, follow the creek's waterfalls until the drainage steepens, then take the steep brushy bushwhack onto the Noyes–Seattle ridge; that brush low down is the crux of that variant, not the scrambling above.
